props.title: The World
props.initialSlug: Romance blooms at a Beijing theme park replica world

sections.content: Jia Zhangke's The World masterfully captures China's rapid modernization through a Beijing theme park filled with miniature global landmarks. Like his earlier Platform (2000) and Unknown Pleasures (2002), Jia uses long takes and minimal camera movement to document China's shift toward capitalism. The film follows performers at World Park, where tourists can see the Eiffel Tower and Twin Towers without leaving Beijing - a perfect metaphor for China's artificial adoption of global culture. The stark contrast between the glamorous show costumes and the performers' dreary daily lives cuts deep.

sections.content: The theme park setting brilliantly represents globalization's impact on Chinese identity. Like Goodbye Dragon Inn (2003) and Yi Yi (2000), the film captures Asian modernity's emotional toll through careful observation. The artificial world of replicas speaks to China's complex relationship with Western influence - simultaneously embracing and keeping it at arm's length. Jia's signature mix of realism and subtle surrealism (including animated sequences) perfectly captures this cultural tension.

The film's focus on migrant workers and performers connects to broader themes in Chinese cinema of the 2000s. Beijing Bicycle (2001) and Last Train Home (2009) similarly examine rural-urban migration and its human cost. But Jia's approach is uniquely meditative, letting scenes unfold naturally while building a powerful portrait of displacement and alienation in modern China. SUBHEAD: Digital Revolution and Urban Alienation

The World marks Jia's first use of digital video, reflecting China's technological transformation. Like Millennium Mambo (2001) and Chungking Express (1994), the film captures urban isolation through its technical choices. The digital aesthetic mirrors the artificial nature of the theme park while allowing intimate access to characters' lives. This technological shift parallels China's own dramatic modernization.
